faq.title: FAQs
faq.q1: How do I arrange a driver?
faq.a1: Send Aris a message on WhatsApp, or fill in the enquiry form, with your dates, where you're staying and what you'd like to do. He'll reply personally to check availability and talk through the details.
faq.a2: Yes. You choose where to go and how long to stay. Aris can suggest places if you'd like ideas, and plans can change on the day where time allows.
faq.q3: How much does a private driver cost?
faq.q4: Can Aris collect us from the airport?
faq.a4: Yes. Airport pickups and drop-offs are one of the main services. Include your flight details when you enquire.
faq.q5: Can he recommend places to visit?
faq.a5: Yes. Tell him what you enjoy, such as food, nature, culture or beaches, and he'll suggest places that suit you.
faq.a6: No. Entry tickets, activities and meals aren't included, and you pay the venues directly. Fuel, parking and toll roads are included in Aris's price.
faq.a7: Yes, families are welcome. Let Aris know how many adults and children are travelling, and the children's ages, so the right arrangements can be made. If you need a child seat, ask when you enquire.
faq.a8: Your booking is confirmed only when Aris confirms it with you personally on WhatsApp, including the final price. Sending an enquiry through this website doesn't create a booking or take payment.
faq.a3: It depends on how long you need a driver and where you'd like to go. See the indicative prices on the Our Services page. Aris confirms the final price before you book.

explore.intro: There's plenty to discover around Bali. From local food and coffee to waterfalls, beaches, adventure and traditional village life. Take a look around and find something that interests you.

a.desc: Bali's interior is a patchwork of rice terraces, jungle valleys, crater lakes and temples. A day of sightseeing usually means a few unhurried stops, with time to walk, take photos and have lunch along the way.

i1.name: Tegallalang Rice Terraces
i1.text: Terraced rice fields in a valley north of Ubud.

i2.name: Ulun Danu Beratan
i2.text: A lakeside water temple in the cool Bedugul highlands.

i3.name: Uluwatu Temple
i3.text: A clifftop temple on the Bukit Peninsula, popular at sunset.

i4.name: Sidemen
i4.text: A quiet valley in East Bali with rice fields and mountain views.

i5.name: Kerta Gosa
i5.text: The historic court pavilion in Klungkung, known for its painted ceilings.

i6.name: Waterfalls
i6.text: Tegenungan, Tibumana and others within reach of Ubud.

b.desc: Some of the best meals in Bali come from small, family-run warungs. Try nasi campur, sate lilit or babi guling, wander through a morning market, or visit a coffee plantation to see how Bali coffee is grown and roasted.

i1.name: Local warungs
i1.text: Simple, family-run eateries serving Balinese and Indonesian dishes.

i2.name: Coffee plantations
i2.text: Tasting stops in the Kintamani highlands and around Ubud.

i3.name: Traditional markets
i3.text: Fresh produce, spices and offerings at local morning markets.

i4.name: Cooking classes
i4.text: Learn to cook Balinese dishes with an independent cooking school.

i5.name: Jimbaran seafood
i5.text: Grilled seafood at tables on the sand at Jimbaran Bay.

i6.name: Cafés
i6.text: Relaxed café culture in Ubud, Canggu and Seminyak.

c.desc: For a more active day, Bali has rivers to raft, jungle trails to ride and a volcano to climb before sunrise. These activities are run by independent operators. Aris can help you choose one and get you there.

i1.name: ATV rides
i1.text: Muddy jungle and rice-field trails, mostly around Ubud.

i2.name: White-water rafting
i2.text: On the Ayung River near Ubud or the Telaga Waja in East Bali.

i3.name: Mount Batur sunrise trek
i3.text: A guided early-morning climb up an active volcano.

i4.name: Water sports
i4.text: Jet skis, parasailing and more at Tanjung Benoa.

i5.name: Surf lessons
i5.text: Beginner-friendly waves at Kuta and Canggu.

i6.name: Snorkelling & diving
i6.text: Clear water around Amed, Padang Bai and Menjangan Island.

d.desc: Travelling with children? Bali has plenty to keep everyone happy, from water slides to calm, shallow beaches. Let Aris know your children's ages and he can help you plan a day with sensible travel times.

i1.name: Waterbom Bali
i1.text: A large water park in Kuta with slides for all ages.

i2.name: Bali Zoo
i2.text: Animal encounters in Singapadu, south of Ubud.

i3.name: Sanur Beach
i3.text: Calm, reef-protected water that suits younger swimmers.

i4.name: Ubud Monkey Forest
i4.text: A forest sanctuary home to long-tailed macaques. Keep bags zipped!

i5.name: Turtle conservation
i5.text: The Turtle Conservation and Education Center on Serangan Island.

i6.name: Nusa Dua
i6.text: Calm beaches and a paved beachfront walkway.

e.desc: Bali's west-facing coast is made for sunsets. Watch the sky change from a clifftop at Uluwatu, have dinner with your feet in the sand at Jimbaran, or find a quieter beach in the south.

i1.name: Uluwatu
i1.text: Clifftop views, surf beaches and the evening Kecak dance at the temple.

i2.name: Jimbaran Bay
i2.text: Seafood dinners on the beach as the sun goes down.

i3.name: Tanah Lot
i3.text: A sea temple on a rocky outcrop, best seen at sunset.

i4.name: Melasti Beach
i4.text: White sand below limestone cliffs on the Bukit Peninsula.

i5.name: Seminyak
i5.text: Beach clubs and sunset bars along the sand.

i6.name: Sanur
i6.text: Bali's sunrise side, with a long beachfront path.

f.desc: Balinese Hindu culture is part of everyday life here: offerings at every doorway, ceremonies in village temples and crafts passed down through families. Please visit respectfully. A sarong and sash are required at temples.

i1.name: Tirta Empul
i1.text: A water temple near Tampaksiring, known for its holy springs.

i2.name: Besakih
i2.text: Bali's largest temple complex, on the slopes of Mount Agung.

i3.name: Penglipuran
i3.text: A traditional village in Bangli, known for its neat layout and bamboo forest.

i4.name: Craft villages
i4.text: Silverwork in Celuk, woodcarving in Mas and painting in Batuan.

i5.name: Traditional dance
i5.text: Evening Legong and Kecak performances in Ubud and at Uluwatu.

i6.name: Ceremonies
i6.text: Temple festivals and processions happen throughout the year. If you come across one, watch quietly from the side.

explore.disclaimer: The places above are independent attractions and destinations. Bali Paradise doesn't operate them or sell their tickets. Aris can drive you there and help you plan your day. Opening hours and entry fees are set by each venue.

local.name: Experience Bali as a Local
local.promise: An in-depth day that explains Bali: offerings, temples, village life, food and the beliefs behind them. Shape it around culture, food, or coffee and the volcano.
local.meta: Full day · about 8–9 hours · by car
local.lead: Most visitors see Bali’s temples and rice fields. Few understand them. Spend the day with Aris and learn why things are the way they are, from someone who lives it.
local.learnTitle: What you'll understand by the end of the day
local.learnLead: Aris explains as you go, in plain English, and there's always time for questions.
local.l1: What canang sari are, who makes them, and why they’re everywhere.
local.l2: How to visit respectfully, and what the shrines, colours and processions mean.
local.l3: The family compound, the banjar (village council) and how a community runs.
local.l4: Why there always seems to be a ceremony, and how the days are chosen.
local.l5: What Balinese families actually eat, and where.
local.l6: Ask anything. That’s the point of the day.
local.dayTitle: A sample day: village and culture
local.d1: Start where locals shop. Try snacks and fruit you won’t find in a supermarket.
local.d2: Coffee and a simple Balinese breakfast.
local.d3: How a family compound works, the household temple and the daily offerings, explained by someone who grew up with them.
local.d5: Sarongs provided. What the shrines, offerings and ceremonies mean.
local.d6: One or two local craftspeople or small family businesses. No commission shopping.
local.d7: Or a drop-off wherever suits you.
local.r1: Kintamani: a local coffee producer and tasting, coffee looking across to Mount Batur, and lunch with the volcano in view. A full day from South Bali.
local.r2: Morning markets, warungs and the dishes Balinese families eat, with the stories behind them.
local.r3: A day planned around temples and, if the calendar allows, a ceremony you can respectfully watch.
local.w4: Anyone who’s done the main sights
local.i1: Private car with fuel, parking and tolls
local.i2: Tastings and warung coffee (coffee tasting on Kintamani days)
local.i5: Pickup in South Bali or Ubud
local.g1: Wear clothes that cover shoulders and knees for temples
local.g2: Ceremony days can change the route; Aris plans around them
local.g3: Bring a light jacket on Kintamani days, the highlands are cooler

solo.lead: Exploring on your own is better with someone who knows the island, speaks your language and genuinely cares that you have a good day.
solo.d1: A first-day orientation, countryside and rice fields, a food morning, or a full day built around what you love.
solo.d2: Money, SIM cards, what to wear, what things should cost. The things that make the rest of your trip easier.
solo.d3: A place most visitors drive straight past.
solo.d4: A local warung and plenty of time to ask anything about Bali.
solo.d5: Your hotel, a café, or the next place you’re staying.
solo.r1: Coffee overlooking the volcano, lunch in Tegallalang and a drop-off in Ubud.
solo.r2: Quiet back roads, rice terraces and a village or two at your own pace.
solo.r3: Markets and warungs you’d never find on your own.
solo.w2: First-timers who want a gentle start
solo.w3: Anyone who prefers a personal day to a big group
solo.i2: Scooter ride with helmet provided, or a car
solo.i3: Coffee and tastings along the way
solo.g1: Pickup and drop-off at reception or the entrance, never inside rooms
solo.g2: Your route is agreed before the day, and you’re welcome to share your live location with someone
solo.g3: Prefer a car? Ask when you enquire
solo.g4: Aris is a licensed rider. Before you travel, check your travel insurance covers riding a scooter as a passenger
solo.g5: Even if you hold an international licence, Aris recommends riding with a local: Balinese roads and traffic rules are very different

consent.label: Cookie choice
consent.text: We use Google Analytics to see which pages help visitors plan their trip. Is that OK? No advertising cookies are used.

reviewForm.title: Tell other travellers about your day
reviewForm.lead: No account needed. Your review is sent to Aris, and genuine reviews appear on the website once he has checked them.
reviewForm.name: Your first name
reviewForm.textPh: What was the day like? Where did you go, and what stood out?
reviewForm.consent: I agree Aris may publish this review on his website with my first name and country.

errors.text: Please write at least a couple of sentences.
errors.consent: Please tick the box so Aris can publish your review.
